ca_frontier_wall.blurb: Frontier Wall is a remote traditional cliff on the west side of Queen Mountain in Joshua Tree National Park. All eleven routes are trad, and the grades lean hard: one 5.7, a few 5.9s, a few 5.10s, and the largest group at 5.11. Crack climbing dominates, which makes it a draw for leaders who want adventurous 5.11 finger and hand cracks rather than bolted faces. The wall looks northwest, so expect shade for much of the day. Getting here means a long walk from the Queen Mountain trailhead, over a low saddle and up a wash, so plan on a committing outing with plenty of water and a full rack.

ca_sidewinder_rock_west_face.blurb: The west face of Sidewinder Rock stands at the mouth of Steve Canyon in the Hidden Valley part of Joshua Tree National Park. It holds about a dozen traditional cracks and face lines, with a distinctive slanting dike running across the upper face. Grades are skewed toward the harder end: a couple of easy lines, a pair around 5.10, five at 5.11 and two at 5.12. Because it faces west, the wall is best in the morning and cools down late in the day. The walk in from the Hidden Valley lot or from roadside turnouts is short, and a bolted rappel from the top of King Pin gets you down.

ca_lyme_disease_rock.blurb: Lyme Disease Rock is a small sandstone crag tucked beside the Indian Rock parking area in the Castle Rock part of the Santa Cruz Mountains. Eleven routes, mostly bolted sport leads with a few top-rope lines, run from easy 5.7 and 5.8 up through a cluster of 5.10s and 5.11s, with one 5.12. The crag is quiet and tidy, and tends to be nearly empty when the bigger walls nearby are busy. Top-rope setups are easy to reach on most lines, so it works for a relaxed session with a mixed group.
ca_lyme_disease_rock.parking_note: Use the free lot outside Indian Rock and walk from there; the rock is a short stroll along the trail.
ca_lyme_disease_rock.approach: From the Indian Rock lot, take the trail to the right for a short distance, roughly a third of a mile. The top of the crag appears on your left; skirt around and drop to the base.

ca_stream_wall.blurb: Stream Wall is a steep little granite cliff in the Horseshoe Piles group above Lake George, near Mammoth Lakes in the Eastern Sierra. At roughly 9,300 feet, it sits next to a creek that flows through most of the season. Routes are shorter but more overhanging than those on the neighboring crags, and the grades run hard: mostly 5.11 and 5.12 with only a few easier outings. The face points southeast, so summer afternoons bring shade. Early in the season the water also brings mosquitoes, which thin out as the creek dries up.
ca_stream_wall.parking_note: Leave the car at the Lake George parking lot and walk from there.
ca_stream_wall.approach: From the lot, climb the Crystal Lake Trail for several minutes to the large water tanks, then head west off the trail over the ridgeline. Traverse the hillside beside the metal pipes to the creek, pass Spring Crag, and continue a couple hundred yards to the wall just beyond the crossing.

ca_tombstones_the_2.blurb: The Tombstones is a short east-facing wall within the Cemetery, a cluster of crags in the high desert near Apple Valley. Most of the eleven routes are bolted sport lines, with one trad crack and one top-rope. Grades cluster between 5.7 and 5.10: a handful of 5.9s, five 5.10s, and a couple of 5.8s. The 5.9s flanking the central crack are described as stiff for the grade, while the 5.10s are fairly rated, so it suits climbers working on that grade. Climbing is steep on thin edges, each route has its own chain anchor, and the wall catches sun for about half of the day.

ca_triceratops_boulder.blurb: Triceratops Boulder is a bouldering spot right on the coast in the Secrets section of Salt Point State Park. It is reached by following the trail to the shoreline and rock-hopping around to the block. Eleven problems range from an easy warm-up and a few V1s up to V5 and V6, with a cluster at V5. The namesake line is a sit start on underclings up a striking prow and is the most popular problem here; holds are sharp. Bring pads, and keep in mind the block sits beside the water, so footing along the approach needs care.

ca_true_summit_block.blurb: True Summit Block caps Bishop Peak above San Luis Obispo, forming the highest point on the mountain. Its eleven routes mix sport, top-rope, a couple of trad lines and one aid line, from 5.5 and 5.6 starters through a middle band at 5.10, a core of 5.11s, and two 5.12s. The climbing is short, around 35 feet on the easiest line, with bolted anchors up top. You get here by hiking the peak's summit trail to the hikers' summit bench and then heading west to the cluster of rocks that looks highest. Expect walkers on the summit nearby.
ca_true_summit_block.approach: Hike to the hikers' summit and continue west to the highest-looking group of rocks; routes begin on the east side of the block.

ca_voodoo_dome_2.blurb: Voodoo Dome is a big, rounded formation in the Needles above the Kern River in the southern Sierra. Its roughly 900-foot bulk is mostly blank rock that gives surprisingly few lines, and it is best known for the classic White Punks on Dope. Eleven routes are listed, almost all trad plus one top-rope, running from a 5.6 chimney through 5.8 and 5.9 to a handful of 5.11s and one 5.12. The approach is longer than the main Needles walk and threads through cairns, and it is reached from the Lloyd Meadow Road side near Johnsondale.
